analysis.one_liner: Requires an annual federal report on foreign investment in America's pharmaceutical and gene-sequencing industries.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 15, 2026 by Senator Elizabeth Warren with one Republican cosponsor, and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Federal Trade Commission, working with the Treasury-led committee that reviews foreign acquisitions of U.S. companies, to publish an annual report on foreign investment in the U.S. pharmaceutical industry. The report must assess whether reliance on foreign manufacturing has weakened America's ability to make drugs and their ingredients, and whether foreign investment in DNA sequencing and storage technologies affects U.S. capacity. It is a transparency measure: it requires studies and a public summary, but it does not ban, restrict, or approve any transaction.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, if it leads to better information about why drugs run short and which foreign buyers are acquiring U.S. drug and gene-sequencing assets. Regulators and lawmakers also gain a factual baseline they currently lack, since the Treasury review committee's decisions are largely confidential.

how_it_helps.text: Requires an annual FTC report, in consultation with the Treasury-run Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, assessing the U.S. pharmaceutical supply chain, the effect of concentration and reliance on foreign manufacturing, and the effect of foreign investment on domestic drug and ingredient production capacity.
Requires the report to cover foreign investment in technologies for sequencing or storing DNA, including genome and exome analysis, and its effect on U.S. sequencing and storage capacity.

Requires disclosure of how many foreign-investment reviews and investigations CFIUS conducted in the pharmaceutical and DNA-sequencing sectors over the prior ten fiscal years, including whether each transaction was approved, prohibited, or approved with conditions.
Requires the FTC to publish an unclassified public summary of the report on its website, so the findings are available to the public rather than only to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, foreign investors seeking U.S. drug or gene-sequencing assets, and the FTC bear the cost: the industry faces sustained scrutiny of its foreign supply relationships, foreign acquirers face a public paper trail of past reviews, and the agency must fund and staff the annual study.

drawbacks.text: The bill only produces information; it does not restrict any transaction, require reshoring, or address drug shortages directly, so it may create the appearance of action without changing outcomes.
The FTC must fund and staff an annual multi-agency study covering supply chains, drug manufacturing, and DNA sequencing, an ongoing administrative expense.

A foreign-investment focus could overlook other drivers of drug shortages, such as domestic market consolidation and low reimbursement prices, and could feed pressure for broad restrictions that raise costs without fixing the underlying problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is modest and mostly falls on industry and agency budgets, while the potential benefit is a public factual record on a supply chain that produced repeated drug shortages. The honest caveat is that a study-only bill guarantees a report, not a fix; its value depends entirely on whether Congress or regulators later act on what it finds.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in July 2026, and with the session running into early January 2027 it has gotten no hearing, markup, or floor vote yet.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 15, 2026, joined by Senator Rick Scott of Florida and Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, giving it one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
The complete action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody has yet: the report it would produce has not been written, and the industries it would scrutinize have avoided no cost. The practical status quo favors drug makers and foreign acquirers, who continue operating without the added public disclosure.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Banking Committee.

for.name: Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 119th Congress by Senator Tim Scott (R-SC)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action on it — no hearing or committee vote appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split evenly at introduction — one Democrat (Warren), one Republican (Scott of Florida), one Democrat (Gillibrand) — and no one has opposed it on the record, though the committee has also not moved it.

industries.note: The bill does not regulate them, but it creates an annual public accounting of their reliance on foreign manufacturing and of foreign buyers of U.S. drug assets, which could build the case for future restrictions or reshoring requirements. Industry flexibility on where it makes drugs and ingredients costs money that the report could make harder to keep quiet.

industries.industry: Foreign investors and acquirers of U.S. drug and biotech assets
industries.note: The report would publish a ten-year record of which foreign investments in pharma and DNA sequencing the Treasury review committee examined, approved, blocked, or conditioned, ending the near-total confidentiality around those decisions in these sectors.

Foreign investment in U.S. DNA sequencing and storage capacity would be assessed annually for its effect on American capability, putting the sector under national-security-style scrutiny it currently receives less systematically.

analysis.trajectory: Report-only bills at this stage rarely get floor time, especially in the final months of a two-year Congress. The bill's best realistic path is being folded into a larger bill moving through the Banking Committee or attached as an amendment, for example to defense or foreign-investment-review legislation; otherwise it will die in committee when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
